title: India Wants Its Diaspora Athletes Back. The Sports Passport Could Make It Happen.
excerpt: With four Indian-origin footballers at the 2026 World Cup and none wearing blue, the Modi government is exploring a fast-track eligibility pathway for OCI and PIO athletes
body:
India's football team may not be at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, but the country's sporting ambitions have never looked more global. The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports has sent a landmark proposal to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's office: a "Sports Passport" that would create a fast-track eligibility pathway for athletes of Indian origin living abroad to represent the country in international competition.

The proposal, confirmed by multiple sources within the ministry, is now under review by both the Prime Minister's Office and the Ministry of Home Affairs. A decision could come within six to eight months.

## Four Men, Four Flags, One Heritage

The urgency of the proposal is underscored by what is unfolding right now across stadiums in the United States, Canada, and Mexico. Four footballers of Indian heritage are at the 2026 FIFA World Cup — representing nations other than India.

**Sarpreet Singh**, a 26-year-old attacking midfielder born in Auckland to Punjabi parents from Jalandhar, is in New Zealand's squad for their Group G campaign. When he takes the field against Iran on June 16 in California, he will become the first player of Indian origin at a men's World Cup since France's Vikash Dhorasoo in 2006. Singh, who once played for FC Bayern Munich's reserves, has spoken openly about what this moment means. "I don't say it's added pressure," he told *Livemint*. "I just want to do my best to lift the names of Indian people, and there is no better stage to do it than the World Cup."

**Tahsin Mohammed Jamshid**, just 19, is in Qatar's squad. His parents, Jamshid and Shaima, hail from Kannur in Kerala and moved to Qatar in 1996. He trained at the Aspire Academy and now plays for Al Duhail. Qatar stunned Switzerland with a 94th-minute equaliser at Levi's Stadium on Saturday — Jamshid was part of the matchday squad.

**Nishan Velupillay** is in Australia's World Cup squad. Born and raised in Melbourne to a father of Sri Lankan Tamil descent with Malaysian roots and an Anglo-Indian mother, he scored on his international debut against China and has earned seven senior caps. Australia beat Turkey 2-0 in Vancouver on Saturday night.

**Samuel Moutoussamy**, who plays for DR Congo, has Indian heritage through his family's roots in the subcontinent.

## The Ryan Williams Precedent

The proposal draws partly from the experience of **Ryan Williams**, the Australian-born footballer who renounced his citizenship in 2025 to acquire an Indian passport and represent the Blue Tigers. Williams debuted under coach Khalid Jamil and scored against Hong Kong. But his path required a total sacrifice — giving up his Australian nationality permanently. India does not permit dual citizenship.

That is precisely the barrier the Sports Passport is designed to lower. Under the proposed framework, eligible Persons of Indian Origin (PIO) and Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) could represent India through a special eligibility pathway without necessarily going through the full citizenship process. The model draws from precedents in Qatar, Bahrain, Turkey, Spain, Hungary, and Austria, all of which have used fast-track mechanisms to strengthen their national teams.

## Why It Matters to NRIs

For the Indian diaspora, the proposal is both practical and symbolic. There are an estimated 32 million people of Indian origin spread across the globe. Many of their children grow up playing football, basketball, tennis, and athletics in countries where these sports have deep infrastructure. India's 2008 ban on OCI cardholders representing the country effectively locked out this talent pool.

A senior ministry official told *KhelNow* that the proposal is aimed at sports where India has been underperforming, with football as a primary focus. But the implications extend far beyond one sport. With India's bid for the 2036 Olympics gaining momentum, the ability to draw on diaspora talent could reshape the country's global sporting footprint.

The Khelo Bharat Niti policy document, unveiled in July 2025, had already signalled this direction: "Wherever feasible, promising and prominent Indian-origin athletes living abroad may be encouraged to come back and play for India at the international level."

## What Happens Next

The government is expected to take six to eight months to reach a decision. The key challenge is legal: amending or working around the Citizenship Act to allow OCI athletes to compete without full naturalization. The Ministry of External Affairs is involved in the discussions, and federations across multiple sports have expressed private interest in expanding their talent pools if regulatory pathways are created.

For now, Indian fans watching the World Cup can cheer for Singh in a New Zealand shirt, Jamshid in Qatar's maroon, and Velupillay in Australian gold. Whether the next generation of Indian-origin athletes will wear blue remains a question for the Prime Minister's desk.
